skills.title: Follow repo conventions, write, then verify with tests
skills.body:
1. list_files near the target path; read any README there.
2. Follow every doc it links (e.g. a style guide) and note required fields, formats, ordering, and schema.
3. Write the file to match those conventions exactly. For lists derived from data, check whether sorting or deduplication is expected.
4. Call run_tests.
5. If it FAILs, inspect the message and compare your file against the docs (missing fields, key order, types, trailing newline, sort order), rewrite the file, and re-run run_tests.
6. Reply DONE only after run_tests passes.

harnesses.rationale: One imperative rule closes the largest cluster: always call run_tests after any edit and before DONE. It is worded to fix failures only by editing the files the task concerns, with no unbounded retry loop. A narrow guardrail blocks the two classic unsafe actions: recursive force-deletes and resets via shell, and reading secret or .env files. This prevents a repeat of the v1 safety rollback without blocking normal reads, writes or test runs. I left the context policy unchanged to avoid side effects.

generations.diagnosis: The largest failure cluster is skipped_verification (6 cases, across the convention and verify families). In each failing trail the worker wrote the output file and stopped without ever calling run_tests. Passing trails followed the same path but then ran run_tests, saw FAIL, and corrected the file (for example, fixing the config fields to match the style guide). The worker can read conventions and write files just fine. What it lacks is a habit of verifying, and a habit of iterating until tests pass before declaring DONE. The verify-1 case shows the same gap: the hostnames were written in source order, possibly unsorted, and nothing checked them.
lessons: Always run run_tests after writing files; a first FAIL is common and tells you exactly what to fix before DONE.
For config tasks, read the directory README and any linked style guide, and match required fields and formats exactly.
When producing derived output (e.g. lists from JSON), verify ordering and format with tests rather than assuming source order is correct.
